overview: Equatorial Guinea became independent from Spain on 12 October 1968. The atlas record begins in 1914, during colonial rule, and connects mainland Río Muni with Bioko. Its early polygon omits distant Annobón, so the outline is incomplete. This is a history of a changing colonial territory and republic, not one culture shared identically by all its communities.

periods.title: Spanish colonial rule
periods.summary: Plantations linked the island and mainland through coercive labour recruitment.

periods.title: Independence and dictatorship
periods.summary: Francisco Macías Nguema’s government became severely repressive.

periods.title: A changed regime and an oil economy
periods.summary: The 1979 coup changed the government; oil later transformed the economy.

items.text: Cocoa plantations on Fernando Po, now Bioko, needed large workforces. Enrique Martino’s archival research traces coercive recruitment from Río Muni and eastern Nigeria between 1926 and 1945. Recruiters, transport networks and colonial officials shaped workers’ lives. A plantation’s output cannot be separated from the conditions under which people were made to produce it.

Spain’s rule ended on 12 October 1968. The diplomatic record subsequently refers to Santa Isabel, the city later called Malabo, as the location of an embassy. Independence created new international relationships, but mainland and island communities retained different histories rather than suddenly becoming culturally interchangeable.

Under Francisco Macías Nguema, political opponents suffered imprisonment and killing. The International Commission of Jurists documented that repression and the military coup of 3 August 1979, led by Teodoro Obiang Nguema. Its trial observer also criticized aspects of the proceedings against Macías. A ruler’s removal did not erase the need for justice.

Oil discoveries in the 1990s brought rapid economic growth. The World Bank’s March 2025 assessment also describes declining oil revenues and inadequate investment in health and education. National income and family well-being are different measures: expensive infrastructure alone does not ensure a good classroom or dependable care.

sections.title: A question, a sculpture and a classroom

items.text: “Yù gò lan mi Pichi?” means “Would you teach me Pichi?” Linguist Kofi Yakpo records this question, including its tone marks, in a study of Pichi. It is a useful first sentence for a visitor who wants to listen and learn, rather than assume that Spanish is everyone’s only language.

Pichi developed from Krio brought to Bioko by African settlers from Freetown in the nineteenth century. Yakpo’s survey describes it as a language of everyday communication across the island, shaped by further migration and contact with Spanish. Its history connects Equatorial Guinea with Sierra Leone and wider coastal networks.

A nineteenth-century Okak-Fang guardian figure in the Met was made from wood, copper alloy and palm oil. Its precise origin is catalogued as Gabon or Equatorial Guinea. Such sculptures stood above bark containers holding ancestors’ relics; the carved figure belonged to a family’s relationship with the dead, not simply to decoration.

During COVID school closures, the programme La Escuela en mi Casa, “School in My Home,” provided distance learning. UNICEF’s 2023 programme document reports that it reached 135,849 students. That is a record of the programme’s reported reach, while a smaller 2022 student survey examined participation and usefulness.

School sanitation remained a serious problem. The same 2023 UNICEF document reported that only 9 percent of schools had handwashing facilities, citing preliminary research that year. A place to wash hands is part of the learning environment, alongside desks, teachers and books; the figure describes that study rather than every later school year.

In October 2025, health and education authorities launched a school-health programme in Bata. Its stated targets included nutrition, mental health, infectious disease and violence affecting pupils. The announcement described a vitamin A pilot in Litoral among initial actions. It was a launch with planned work, not proof that all schools already had those services.

Bioko has also contributed original malaria research. A study published in 2025 compared different levels of indoor insecticide spraying during 2021 and 2022, checking infections with rapid tests in annual household surveys. The researchers asked how to protect communities effectively with limited resources, testing an operational question rather than assuming more spraying always answers it.

In 2018 the Bioko Marine Turtle Program attached satellite transmitters to six green turtles to study their journeys and feeding grounds. Local field assistants also worked at nesting-season camps. Following a turtle after it leaves the beach helps researchers understand why protection must extend beyond the patch of sand where its eggs were laid.

ending.text: Spanish rule ended in 1968, and the 1979 coup replaced a government rather than ending the republic. Equatorial Guinea continues, with distinct island and mainland communities and ongoing questions about public services and the distribution of resource wealth.
